summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the United States federal framework applies on the island in full: federal statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, federally funded care and federal custody. Puerto Rico's own legislation does not soften that framework, and in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a marker that does not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminalised in Puerto Rico. The Puerto Rico Supreme Court upheld the territory's sodomy ban in 2002; the United States Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 invalidated state and territorial sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, and Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for that care, and set penalties of up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent loss of medical licences for doctors who violate the ban. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

The care law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment, but the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any United States jurisdiction according to the report documenting it.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The first hate crime charges in Puerto Rico's history were brought in 2020, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; Bonilla confessed to the killings. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage remains partial. The 2013 law that passed (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered by it. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Refusal of service on gender-identity grounds remains a live risk in settings where no ordinance fills the gap left by that statute. In April 2019 Governor Ricardo Rosselló announced Senate Bill 1253, framed as clarifying religious freedom principles, alongside Senate Bill 1254, a conversion-therapy ban carrying a pastoral exemption; Johanne Velez Garcia, president of the territory's LGBT council, and allied advocates said the pairing would open doors to discrimination, treating the religious-freedom carve-out as licence to refuse service on orientation or gender-identity grounds. Rosselló asked lawmakers to withdraw both bills on 13 June 2019 amid sustained opposition. A comparable religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Rosselló in February 2018.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples in Puerto Rico was won through federal court rather than local statute. The challenge filed in March 2014, the Ada Conde Vidal case, drew intervention from Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas, and in June 2014 four couples joined as plaintiffs, among them a former National Guard member and two couples already married in Canada in 2007 and New York in 2012.

Under Executive Order 14168, which directs United States federal agencies to recognise only two sexes, the Bureau of Prisons houses transgender inmates by sex assigned at birth rather than asserted gender identity, a rule that governs any federal custody in Puerto Rico. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting how many transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order contravenes the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided by individual safety assessment.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2025 care statute is described by the report documenting it as the most extreme restriction on trans medical care in any United States jurisdiction, which places Puerto Rico at the outer edge of a national pattern of state and territorial youth-care bans rather than in the middle of it.

Legislative attempts to constrain LGBTQ protections have repeatedly failed or been withdrawn. The pro-statehood NPP caucus in the Puerto Rico House blocked a floor vote on Senate Bill 1000 in March 2019, killing a conversion-therapy ban for minors despite Senate passage and the governor's support, with co-sponsor Senator Zoe Laboy publicly dissenting. The governor then withdrew the paired religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills on 13 June 2019 after House approval and sustained protest.

Marriage equality arrived by federal litigation in 2014 while the territorial legislature produced no statute of its own, a contrast with jurisdictions where recognition was enacted locally. The wider anti-discrimination bill of 2009 died in the Senate without hearings, and the narrowed 2013 law is the only measure that reached the governor's signature.
localsOnly:
Conversion therapy for minors is not banned in Puerto Rico: Senate Bill 1000 failed in the House in March 2019 and the replacement measure, Senate Bill 1254, was withdrawn in June 2019, so the practice remains unregulated by territorial statute.

Residents are covered by the 2013 employment-discrimination law only. House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extended domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity, giving residents a route to protection in intimate-partner violence that the employment statute does not provide.

Trans residents under 21 are barred from gender-affirming care and public funding for it is prohibited, with clinicians facing up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent licence loss. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation has announced a court challenge to the statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections policy on housing transgender inmates, dedicated unit, or judicial ruling on the question was located in the sources, so territorial custody practice beyond the federal Bureau of Prisons rule is unresolved.

The outcome of the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation's announced legal challenge to the July 2025 care statute is not sourced here; whether any court has enjoined or upheld the law remains unresolved.

Enforcement of the 2013 employment-discrimination law on gender-identity grounds, and the current status of any litigation over the X marker on United States travel documents, are not documented in the available inventory.
